name: Conditional Lower Bounds and Barriers for Subset Sum
description: This item collects the conditional lower bounds, fine-grained reductions, and hardness hypotheses that constrain exact subset sum and thus define what a hypothetical O*(2^{n/3}) algorithm would and would not contradict. Unlike NP-completeness, which only says no polynomial algorithm unless P=NP, fine-grained complexity conditions the exponent itself. The relevant assumptions are: ETH (no 2^{o(n)} algorithm for 3-SAT, hence none for non-sparse subset sum); SETH and its variants; the k-SAT-to-dense-Subset-Sum reduction of Abboud, Bringmann, Hermelin and Shabtay, which makes Bellman's O*(T) pseudo-polynomial algorithm conditionally optimal up to a T^{1-epsilon} * 2^{o(n)} factor; the k-SUM conjecture (no randomized O(n^{ceil(k/2)-epsilon}) algorithm), which predicts meet-in-the-middle optimality for k-SUM; the 3SUM conjecture (no truly subquadratic algorithm); the (min,+)-convolution hypothesis, tied to knapsack by Cygan-Mucha-Wegrzycki-Wlodarczyk and by Kuennemann-Paturi-Schneider; and the Orthogonal Vectors conjecture. The formal/empirical 'Meet-in-the-Middle barrier' for subset sum -- no O*(2^{(1/2-epsilon)n}) worst-case algorithm -- is a conjecture rather than a theorem; in Randolph's 2024 thesis it is treated with the dignity of a fine-grained hypothesis and even stated optimistically as a conjecture that subset sum CAN be solved in 2^{(0.5-epsilon)n}. The crucial takeaway: current assumptions rule out 2^{o(n)} (ETH) and pin the pseudo-polynomial T-dependence (SETH), but none of them is known to force a 2^{Omega(n)} lower bound with a constant below 1/2, so a 2^{n/3} algorithm would be a major breakthrough yet would not falsify any established hypothesis.
worst_case_time: Best proven worst-case upper bound: O*(2^{n/2}) (Horowitz-Sahni 1974), with only polynomial-factor improvement to O(2^{n/2}/n^{gamma}) for a constant gamma >= 0.5023 (Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio, APPROX/RANDOM 2023; randomized). Conditional lower bounds: under ETH no 2^{o(n)} algorithm; under SETH no T^{1-epsilon} * 2^{o(n)} algorithm for n items and target T (Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay, SODA 2019 / TALG 2022); under the k-SUM conjecture no randomized O(n^{ceil(k/2)-epsilon}) algorithm for k-SUM; under the 3SUM conjecture no truly subquadratic 3SUM; under the (min,+)-convolution hypothesis no truly subquadratic (min,+) convolution. No unconditional 2^{Omega(n)} lower bound for subset sum is known beyond NP-hardness.
space_complexity: Not applicable to the lower bounds themselves. For context, the best space for a 2^{n/2}-time algorithm is O*(2^{n/4}) (Schroeppel-Shamir 1981), improved to O*(2^{0.249999n}) (Nederlof-Wegrzycki, STOC 2021) and O*(2^{0.246n}) (Belova et al., ESA 2024); space is an independent axis from the time-exponent barrier.
model: Word RAM / random-access machine and Turing machine for the algorithmic upper bounds; fine-grained reductions over these models for the conditional lower bounds. Randomized vs deterministic matters: the k-SUM conjecture is explicitly about randomized algorithms succeeding with high probability, while SETH/ETH-based bounds apply to both deterministic and randomized algorithms.
randomized_or_deterministic: The conditional lower bounds generally rule out both deterministic and randomized algorithms (the k-SUM conjecture targets randomized algorithms succeeding w.h.p.). The current best upper bound 2^{n/2}/n^{gamma} is randomized/Monte Carlo (CJR+S 2023), whereas classical MITM and Schroeppel-Shamir are deterministic.
time_space_tradeoff_curve: The barrier concerns the time exponent 1/2 and is orthogonal to space: Schroeppel-Shamir give time O(2^n/S^2) for any space budget S <= O*(2^{n/4}); space can be driven down to 2^{0.246n} while the time exponent stays 0.5. No time-space tradeoff family crosses the 1/2 time exponent.
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: Time exponent record: 0.5 (Horowitz-Sahni 1974; Schroeppel-Shamir 1981 kept 0.5 with far less space). Only polynomial shaving is known: 2^{n/2}/n^{gamma}, gamma >= 0.5023 (Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio 2023). Space exponent record: 0.246 (Belova et al., ESA 2024). No confirmed time exponent strictly below 0.5 for worst-case vanilla subset sum.
problem_variant: Vanilla exact/decision Subset Sum (dense instances for the SETH bound), Equal Subset Sum / Subset Balancing, Partition (C={-1,0,1}), k-SUM, 3SUM, (min,+)-convolution, Orthogonal Vectors, and parameterized k-SUM (k part of the parameter). Cardinality-constrained / fixed-Hamming-weight variants inherit the same barriers.
applies_to: Worst-case exact subset sum. The SETH-based lower bound already applies to dense instances (large target), which is the hard regime for pseudo-polynomial methods. The meet-in-the-middle barrier is stated for the general worst case and the promise-free decision problem; it is density-agnostic for the exponent.
coefficient_set: C = {0,1} for vanilla subset sum, so |C| = 2. Generalized/balancing variants use C subset of Z, e.g., C={-1,0,1} for Equal Subset Sum / Partition. k-SUM has no coefficient restriction (one item chosen from each of k lists).
density_regime: The MITM barrier is density-agnostic (it bounds the 2^{n/2} enumeration regardless of density). The SETH T^{1-epsilon}2^{o(n)} lower bound holds for dense instances, the regime where Bellman's pseudo-polynomial algorithm is the relevant competitor. Low-density knapsacks admit lattice/reduction attacks (LLL/BKZ, Lagarias-Odlyzko), but those are average-case or heuristic and do not yield worst-case hardness or algorithms.
solution_regime: General decision with no promise. Pigeonhole / numerous-solution variants (Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum, Equal Subset Sum) admit algorithms below the MITM baseline, showing the barrier is regime-specific and does not automatically transfer to promised-solution versions.
cardinality_constraint: A fixed Hamming weight can be imposed cheaply (adding a 0-value item lifts subset sum to a fixed-cardinality instance), so cardinality-constrained subset sum is at least as hard and inherits the meet-in-the-middle and SETH barriers. Cardinality is relevant because balanced solutions are the hardest case for MITM.
key_technique: Fine-grained reductions and equivalences: k-SAT -> dense Subset Sum (SETH); OR-Subset-Sum and AND-Subset-Sum / Direct-OR theorems; (min,+)-convolution <-> Unbounded Knapsack (and 0-1 Knapsack); 3SUM reductions; k-SUM meet-in-the-middle with the k-SUM conjecture; Orthogonal Vectors; and the formalization of a Meet-in-the-Middle optimality statement as a fine-grained hypothesis.
core_idea: Every known barrier is conditional: each hypothesis (ETH, SETH, k-SUM, 3SUM, min-plus convolution, OV) rules out a family of algorithms. Because subset sum is not known to be tightly equivalent to any single core problem at the level of the exponential exponent, the exact complexity between 2^{o(n)} and 2^{n/2} is not pinned down. The MITM barrier is a conjecture, and ETH/SETH/3SUM/min-plus do not imply a constant-below-1/2 exponent lower bound. A 2^{n/3} algorithm would therefore be a breakthrough but would refute only the (informal) claim that 2^{(1/2-epsilon)n} is impossible -- not ETH, SETH, 3SUM, min-plus, or NP != P.
reduction_pipeline: k-SAT -> dense Subset Sum (Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay) yields the SETH lower bound and the Direct-OR theorem; (min,+)-convolution -> Unbounded Knapsack and back (Cygan-Mucha-Wegrzycki-Wlodarczyk; independently Kuennemann-Paturi-Schneider) ties knapsack to a quadratic MinConv barrier; 3SUM <-> many geometric/weighted problems (Gajentaan-Overmars, modern Patrascu/Vassilevska Williams formulation); k-SUM is the natural MITM target for subset sum and other reductions; OV conjecture under SETH.
constructive_vs_existential: The lower bounds are conditional/existential: they assert that no algorithm of a certain complexity class exists if a hypothesis holds. The reductions used to derive them are explicit and constructive, but they do not construct an unconditionally hard instance.
search_vs_decision_witness: Most statements concern the decision problem; the search/witness version is at least as hard. Some bounds (AND-Subset-Sum, Direct-OR) explicitly involve deciding whether one out of many instances is a YES instance, a strengthening relevant to search and to scheduling applications.
obstacle_to_2n3: There is no unconditional obstacle. ETH only forbids 2^{o(n)}, which a 2^{n/3} algorithm satisfies. The SETH-based subset-sum bound is about the pseudo-polynomial dependence (no T^{1-epsilon} * 2^{o(n)}) and permits 2^{Omega(n)} algorithms. The 3SUM, k-SUM, and (min,+)-convolution conjectures are not known to imply a 2^{Omega(n)} lower bound for subset sum (no tight exponential-exponent reduction is known). The only statement a 2^{(1/3)n} algorithm would contradict is the explicit Meet-in-the-Middle optimality hypothesis (no O*(2^{(1/2-epsilon)n}) algorithm), which is unproven and, in Randolph's thesis, even framed as an optimistic conjecture that subset sum CAN be solved in 2^{(0.5-epsilon)n}. The precise obstacle is thus the absence of a reduction making subset sum equivalent to 3SUM/k-SUM/OV/MinConv at the exponential-exponent level.
potential_to_break_mitm: Low as a route to breaking MITM -- this is a barrier line, and its role is to delimit which methods are ruled out. Its diagnostic value is high: it shows the MITM barrier is soft (not implied by any established hypothesis), so a 2^{n/3} algorithm is not blocked by current theory, only by the lack of a technique and by the specific, unproven MITM conjecture.
barrier_evidence: ETH: subset sum has no 2^{o(n)} algorithm (Impagliazzo-Paturi). SETH: Bellman's O*(T) cannot be improved to T^{1-epsilon} * 2^{o(n)} (Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay, SODA 2019 / TALG 2022), with Direct-OR and AND-Subset-Sum corollaries. k-SUM conjecture: no randomized O(n^{ceil(k/2)-epsilon}) for k-SUM (Abboud-Lewi, ICALP 2013), implying MITM optimality for k-SUM. 3SUM conjecture: no truly subquadratic 3SUM. (min,+)-convolution hypothesis: no truly subquadratic (min,+) convolution, equivalent to subquadratic Unbounded Knapsack (Cygan et al.; Kuennemann-Paturi-Schneider). Orthogonal Vectors conjecture under SETH. On the algorithmic side, the best worst-case bound remains 2^{n/2}/n^{gamma} (CJR+S 2023), and MITM has resisted an exponent improvement for 50 years.
open_questions: Can ETH or SETH be strengthened to rule out 2^{(1/2-epsilon)n} (or even 2^{(1-epsilon)n}) for subset sum? Is there a tight reduction between subset sum and k-SUM or Orthogonal Vectors that transfers those conjectures to the exponential exponent? Is the Meet-in-the-Middle barrier provable under any standard assumption, or only an empirical regularity? Does the subset-balancing progress (Randolph-Wegrzycki 2025 / STOC 2026) extend to C={0,1} vanilla subset sum? Can the (min,+)-convolution equivalence be lifted from pseudo-polynomial knapsack to the exponential subset-sum regime? What is the exact relative complexity of Equal-Subset-Sum and subset sum?
conditional_hypothesis: ETH (Impagliazzo-Paturi 1999/2001), SETH and forall-exists-SETH, the k-SUM conjecture (Abboud-Lewi 2013), the 3SUM conjecture, the (min,+)-convolution hypothesis, the Orthogonal Vectors conjecture, and the informal/formal Meet-in-the-Middle (Subset Sum) hypothesis. The last is not a standard assumption and is sometimes framed in the opposite (optimistic) direction.
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: All barriers are worst-case statements. The average-case picture differs sharply: average-case Equal Subset Sum / Subset Balancing is solvable in O(3^{0.387n}) (Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio, SODA 2022), below the average-case MITM benchmark, and recent worst-case algorithms beat MITM for broad coefficient sets (Randolph-Wegrzycki 2025). This shows the barrier is specific to worst-case vanilla subset sum.
cryptographic_regime: Highly relevant. The SETH-based T^{1-epsilon} * 2^{o(n)} lower bound is the theoretical basis for the security margin of knapsack-based cryptosystems (e.g., Merkle-Hellman type) and matches the practical attack complexity; density~1 random knapsacks are the cryptanalytic hard case, where MITM is the standard attack. At low density, lattice (LLL/BKZ) attacks apply, so the conditional hardness is regime-dependent. The barriers bound feasible key sizes under the assumptions stated.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: Central. Bellman's O(nT) pseudo-polynomial algorithm is conditionally optimal in its T-dependence under SETH (no T^{1-epsilon} * 2^{o(n)}). Bringmann-Fischer-Nakos (SODA 2025) beat Bellman in all regimes for the output-sensitive parameter |S(X,t)| but do not contradict SETH. The (min,+)-convolution equivalence ties Unbounded Knapsack to a quadratic barrier. Any 2^{n/3} algorithm would have to beat these pseudo-polynomial methods precisely in the dense regime where the SETH bound lives, while remaining consistent with it (since 2^{n/3} is not 2^{o(n)} * T^{1-epsilon} for polynomial T).

empirical_evidence: None found: this is a theory/fine-grained-complexity item. The supporting 'evidence' is the body of reductions and the 50-year absence of a worst-case exponent improvement over 2^{n/2}.
verification_method: Check the SETH reduction from k-SAT to dense Subset Sum and its T^{1-epsilon} * 2^{o(n)} corollary in Abboud et al.; verify the (min,+)-convolution <-> Unbounded Knapsack equivalence in Cygan et al. and Kuennemann-Paturi-Schneider; verify the k-SUM conjecture statement and its MITM matching bound in Abboud-Lewi; and inspect Conjecture 1 in Randolph's thesis for the exact Meet-in-the-Middle conjecture formulation and its optimistic direction.
